Caption: Most IAM reviews focus on individual permissions. But attackers don't think that way. They look for combinations. A permission that appears harmless on its own can become dangerous when combined with another permission elsewhere in the environment. Consider examples like: • KMS Decrypt + S3 Read • Secrets Manager Access + Lambda Update • CloudTrail Stop Logging + IAM Modification • S3 Policy Changes + Bucket Read/Write Individually, these permissions may not trigger major concern. Together, they can create a direct path to data exposure, privilege escalation, or reduced visibility during an attack. This is one of the biggest challenges in cloud security today. Most tools identify individual findings. Few analyze how permissions interact across identities, resources, and services to create hidden attack paths. Securitain was built to address exactly this problem. By analyzing IAM permissions, trust relationships, resource access, and toxic permission combinations, Securitain helps AWS teams uncover risks that may remain hidden in traditional security reviews. Because the real risk is often not a single permission. Caption: Innovation Or Better Marketing? A new AI infrastructure battle is heating up. Databricks recently unveiled its LTAP architecture, calling it the first system to combine transactional and analytical databases into a single copy. SingleStore wasn't impressed. CEO Raj Verma quickly pushed back, arguing that SingleStore has offered the same capability for years and already serves hundreds of customers using it. The company's response was blunt: "We didn't announce it. We shipped it, seven years ago." SingleStore also challenged Databricks' open-source narrative, claiming the architecture creates deeper customer lock-in. Here's what most people miss: In tech, winning isn't always about inventing first. It's often about owning the narrative. Many breakthrough technologies become famous only when a larger player enters the market. Real question: What matters more in technology: being first to build it, or being the company that convinces the world it matters? Caption: Trust is usually treated like a brand issue, but in modern marketing it is also tied closely to how well the business is organized behind the scenes. A company can have a good logo, a polished website, and strong visuals, but still create a weak customer experience if the systems behind the marketing are disconnected. You see this when an ad sends people to a page that does not match the offer, when an inquiry form does not trigger the right follow-up, when customer information sits in the wrong place, or when the sales conversation feels disconnected from what the marketing promised. Customers may not see the system behind the business, but they feel the result of it. They feel it when the response is slow, when the next step is unclear, when the message changes from one place to another, or when the business does not feel as organized after the inquiry as it did before. That is why marketing infrastructure matters. The website, CRM, email follow-up, lead handling, advertising, content, automation, and reporting should work together as one connected customer journey. When those pieces are aligned, the business has more control over what happens after someone shows interest. This is where modern marketing systems become valuable. They do not just help a business move faster. They help the business respond more consistently, manage leads more properly, and create a stronger experience from first impression to follow-up. For businesses that want to grow, the goal is not just to generate more attention. The goal is to make sure the system behind the attention is strong enough to support the customer when they are ready to move forward. Businesses that maintain a consistent content strategy generate 67% more leads per month than those that do not. Not from increasing ad spend. From expertise that works while they sleep. The businesses I see winning are rarely the ones with the single best product in their category. They are the ones prospects find first, trust fastest, and remember longest. Marketing is not a cost center sitting separately from the business. It is the mechanism that makes every other part of the business possible to sell. The founder who gave up after one failed ad campaign was not wrong that his first attempt did not work. He was wrong to conclude that meant the channel did not work. Caption: Being an employee was never really my thing. For years I’ve been trying to build something of my own, different attempts, different paths, different failures and successes. But things don’t always go the way we want. So I reached a point where I had to start a job again. I like the experience it brings, but the conditions? Not working for me at all. Shifts during weekends for a person like me who believes in work-life balance, who is living away from her hometown and is genuinely alive through her connections and friends, losing the chance of seeing any human being in person during a whole week was far away from my thoughts and expectations. Also the salary sucks and there is no perk and leave at all! But this is the fact of my life right now. I am not complaining. I am sharing this because I know I am not alone in this. Many people, especially founders, are living this double life. Building something meaningful on the side while paying their bills somewhere else. So don’t feel bad or embarrassed if you are experiencing the same, and don’t be surprised when you see a founder with an “Open to Work” badge on their LinkedIn profile. That’s not failure. That’s just the part nobody posts about. I chose this path consciously. Not because I had no options, but because building something meaningful takes time, and time needs stability. The job is the bridge. What I’m building is the destination. If you’re somewhere in this same messy in-between, building on the side, figuring it out, holding two lives at once, my DM is open. Caption: The coding mistake that is making your company’s data cleaning 100 times too slow. 🛑💻 Imagine having to reprint an entire 500-page textbook just because you needed to change a single sentence on page 20. It sounds ridiculous, but that is exactly how old data storage systems handle modifications. When an AI dataset needs to remove old, private, or incorrect information, it routinely rewrites massive files just to delete a few rows. Upgrading to Apache Iceberg v3 introduces a feature called Deletion Vectors. Instead of rewriting the whole file, the system simply creates a tiny digital "sticky note" that tells the AI to skip specific lines. Deleting data literally becomes as fast as flipping a single switch. But beware: if your processing software isn't updated to read these smart new notes, it will keep doing things the slow, expensive way. Stop running outdated infrastructure. Caption: Pedi ao Gemini que criasse uma imagem para ilustrar um problema que eu estava enfrentando: processar IA dentro da própria API. Em um fluxo financeiro, isso acontece quando o usuário envia um relatório, uma nota de corretagem ou um extrato para leitura automática. Se OCR, LLM, classificação e extração rodam dentro da requisição, a API fica presa esperando o processamento terminar. Resultado: timeout, fila invisível, usuário travado na tela e risco de quebra quando mais arquivos entram ao mesmo tempo. A solução é separar recebimento de processamento: a API recebe o arquivo, cria um job_id e responde rápido. O trabalho pesado vai para uma fila, é processado em background e o resultado pode ser consultado depois. Na prática, isso transforma uma API frágil em uma arquitetura mais escalável para produção. Caption: Коли рекомендація блогера стає продажем? 🌟 Інфлюенсери впливають на покупки частіше, ніж здається. Але найчастіше вони не створюють потребу, а допомагають зробити вибір. 👀 Найбільший вплив рекомендації мають тоді, коли людина вже замислювалася про покупку. Також важливо, щоб блогер сам давно та регулярно користувався продуктом. Для частини аудиторії додатковим стимулом стають спеціальні пропозиції та промокоди, а для інших – рекомендації в нових для себе категоріях. І це не лише теорія. 📊 28% українців уже купували товари або послуги за рекомендацією блогера. Втім, шлях до покупки не завжди прямий. Після реклами в контенті блогерів хтось просто переглядає інтеграцію, хтось переходить за посиланням із цікавості, а дехто зберігає інформацію, щоб повернутися до неї пізніше. Лише частина аудиторії одразу взаємодіє з брендом. 💡 Інфлюенсер-маркетинг працює не лише через миттєві продажі. Часто рекомендація стає ще одним аргументом, який допомагає споживачу впевнитися у своєму виборі.

Caption: Рекомендації блогерів: що формує довіру? 👤🤳🏼 На конференції IAB Connect 2026: «Диджитал і Конструктив» Клієнт-партнерка Kantar Україна Оля Капустян представила результати дослідження «Коли рекомендація стає продажем: як інфлюенсери та стрімери впливають на вибір українців». За даними Kantar, 79% українців сьогодні слідкують за контентом інфлюенсерів. Для багатьох це не лише розвага, а й спосіб дізнатися щось нове та орієнтуватися у новинках брендів. 👀 Та чи довіряють українці рекомендаціям блогерів? Лише 17% українців довіряють рекламі інфлюенсерів, тоді як майже половина займає нейтральну позицію. 🤝🏻 Найбільше на довіру впливають чесність, тривалий контакт з автором та відсутність надмірної реклами. Натомість вона швидко руйнується, коли реклама виглядає нещирою або створює відчуття «занадто ідеальної» картинки. 💡 Для брендів це важливий сигнал: аудиторія очікує від інфлюенсерів не бездоганної реклами, а чесних і релевантних рекомендацій.

Caption: One sentence from this week's newsletter has been stuck in my head. The business is simply a tool. Your life is the destination. I think a lot of aspiring entrepreneurs skip over that idea. They spend hours researching business ideas, watching YouTube videos, listening to podcasts, and trying to figure out which opportunity has the most potential. That matters, but what matters more is the kind of life you actually want. A business can be profitable and still be a poor fit. If you value flexibility, certain businesses will naturally fit better than others. If your goal is building a large company, you'll make different decisions than someone who wants to stay small and work directly with clients. If spending time with your family is one of your highest priorities, that should influence the type of business you build. There isn't one version of entrepreneurial success. There are thousands. The important part is choosing yours before you start chasing someone else's. Caption: Agentic AI is about to get a lot harder to turn off. The "loopy" shift in AI isn't just a fun buzzword. It's a real architectural change. Instead of one agent doing a task and stopping, you now have swarms of agents running continuously in the background — looping, delegating, self-correcting. This is where things get genuinely interesting for builders. Right now most people are still thinking about AI as a request-response tool. You prompt it, it answers. That mental model is already outdated. The loop model means you're not building a feature anymore. You're building a system that runs autonomously, makes decisions without you, and keeps going. That's a different responsibility entirely. The real questions developers need to answer now: How do you monitor something that never stops? How do you know when it's doing something wrong? What does "done" even mean when the agent is designed to keep going? These aren't theoretical problems. If you're building anything with Claude Code or multi-agent setups right now, you're already bumping into early versions of this. The teams that figure out observability, error handling, and trust boundaries for continuous agents — those are the teams that will actually ship reliable products. Everyone else will have impressive demos that break in production. I've been thinking a lot about this for my own builds. The jump from "agent that completes a task" to "agent that runs forever" is not a small one. What's your current approach to keeping agents under control when they're running autonomously? Caption: You did everything right. Migrated to Databricks. Enabled Photon. Hit run. And your PySpark job… took the exact same time. 😶 Plot twist: Photon was never even running your code. Here's what's actually happening 👇 Photon is Databricks' blazing-fast, C++-based execution engine. It's vectorized, SIMD-optimized, and genuinely powerful — but only for native Spark SQL operations. The moment you drop a Python UDF into your pipeline? Spark bypasses Photon entirely. It serializes your data into Python objects, runs the function row by row in the Python runtime, then brings results back. All that overhead? Photon can't help. The culprit is hiding in plain sight inside your .withColumn() calls. The fix that changes everything: Replace Python UDFs → Native Spark SQL built-ins OR Arrow-based Pandas UDFs. That's it. 5 minutes of refactoring. 2–10x speed gains. This is the kind of thing that separates good data engineers from great ones — knowing why a tool isn't working, not just that it isn't. 📖 Full article with working code fix in bio link 👇 👉 Follow for weekly deep-dives into Spark, Databricks, and data engineering 🔥 PySpark Databricks DataEngineering ApacheSpark PhotonEngine BigDataAnalytics SparkOptimization PythonDeveloper DataPipeline TechTips DataScience LearnToCode

Caption: One of the biggest mistakes people make when exploring tech careers is assuming every data role does the same thing. They do not. Data Analytics, Data Science, and Data Engineering may all work with data, but they solve completely different problems. A Data Analyst helps businesses understand what happened and why. They turn raw information into reports, dashboards, and actionable insights that support decision making. A Data Scientist goes a step further. They use statistics, machine learning, and predictive models to answer questions about what is likely to happen next. A Data Engineer focuses on the foundation. They build the systems, pipelines, and infrastructure that make data available, reliable, and usable for everyone else. If you enjoy communicating insights and working closely with business teams, Data Analytics may be the right fit. If you enjoy statistics, machine learning, and predictive modelling, Data Science could be your path. If you enjoy building systems, solving technical challenges, and working behind the scenes, Data Engineering may be the best option. The good news? All three are in demand. The better news? Caption: 📊 We tracked 1,600 posts to see what an influencer collab actually does to engagement. The data had a plot twist. 👇 We built a single "weighted engagement" score for every post → likes + (comments × 2), because a comment takes more effort than a like, so it should count more. Then we smoothed the noise with two lines: 📈 Rolling mean = the average engagement over a moving 30-day window (sensitive to viral outliers). 📉 Rolling median = the typical post in that same window (ignores the viral spikes; the more honest "normal day" line). The reveal? Engagement didn't peak during the March collab - it kept climbing and peaked in mid-June, ~3 months later 🤯. The collab window sits on the slope up, not the summit. Both the average AND the typical post agree on June, so this isn't just one viral post skewing things. Takeaway for brands: the impact of a collab isn't always instant and the spike you celebrate might not be the one that matters. Look at the trend, not the moment. 🔍 ⚠️ The fine print (because good data has caveats): • No follower data → we measured raw engagement, not engagement rate. If the audience grew, some of this shift is just reach, not performance. • Correlation ≠ causation → June could be a seasonal launch, another campaign, or sheer virality. We can't pin the peak on any single cause. • Hidden likes & outliers → a few mega-viral posts pull the mean hard; that's exactly why we plotted the median too. Data tells better stories when you respect what it can't say. 💬 What would you want us to analyze next? Caption: The difference between a workflow that runs and a workflow that survives production? Design discipline. A fintech ops team built a 140-node KYC pipeline in Autonoly. It ran perfectly for 11 months — through 3 API provider changes, 2 compliance updates, and a migration from Postgres to BigQuery. Not a single unplanned outage. When we asked how, their automation lead said: "We follow 10 rules religiously." Here they are: 1. One workflow, one purpose — scope creep kills reliability 2. Name every node descriptively — "transform_invoice_to_xero_format" beats "step_7" 3. Handle errors at every step — not just the happy path 4. Use variables, never hardcode — one config change updates 50 workflows 5. Test with real data before launch — synthetic data hides real-world edge cases 6. Set timeouts on all API calls — a hanging node can cascade into a full pipeline freeze 7. Log inputs and outputs — you cannot debug what you cannot see 8. Version your workflows — rollback should take 10 seconds, not 10 hours 9. Keep branches under 3 levels deep — complexity is technical debt with compound interest 10. Document the "why," not just the "what" — intent outlives implementation Rule 4 alone saved them 80+ hours of manual updates after their payment gateway switched endpoints. Caption: Prompt engineering improves the first response. Loop engineering improves the final outcome. As AI coding agents take on more complex software tasks, a strong prompt is no longer enough. Real projects require agents to work through a structured cycle: Plan → Search → Modify → Verify → Repair → Summarise This is the idea behind Loop Engineering: designing AI workflows where agents use tests, logs, compiler errors, code reviews, and human feedback to continuously improve their work. A well-designed loop helps teams: • Reduce unverified AI-generated code • Make smaller, reversible changes • Detect wrong assumptions early • Improve reliability through continuous validation • Keep humans in control of product and architectural decisions The next generation of AI-enabled teams will not compete only on who writes better prompts. Caption: Voice agents are about to feel different. Nvidia Nemotron ASR Streaming is the new listening layer for any ai voice agent stack. Real time transcription with cache aware FastConformer RNNT architecture, which means it does not waste cycles re-listening to audio it has already processed. The result is lower latency, cleaner transcripts, and a voice product that feels like a conversation instead of a walkie talkie. Two variants ship out of the box. English only for tight latency on en US workloads. Multilingual for 40 language locales with automatic language detection in a single checkpoint. That retires the per language ASR routing layer most global support teams have been stitching together for years. Why this matters right now. ASR latency compounds through every step of a voice agent. Planner, action layer, text to speech, transport. Shave time off the listening layer and the entire interaction speeds up. Multilingual coverage is no longer optional. The multilingual variant collapses a routing problem into a model call. Deployment is a NIM container, not a six month infrastructure project. What a serious rollout looks like. Pick the variant for your language coverage. Smoke test on real production audio. Measure microphone to first token latency, not just model latency. Wire the transcript into whatever consumes it next. Planner, summarizer, CRM, downstream LLM. Monitor word error rate, latency percentiles, and task success. Optimize against task success. Teams that anchor their voice strategy on a streaming first ASR engine this year will have a head start. Voice is finally ready to feel real. Caption: ☸️ Most ML engineers avoid Kubernetes because it looks intimidating. But avoiding it doesn't make it go away, it just makes you dependent on someone else who understands it. Here's Kubernetes for ML in 5 minutes 👇 Docker runs one container. Kubernetes runs hundreds of containers reliably, with scaling, self-healing, and automation built in. Why ML workloads need K8s: ⚡ GPU-intensive → Resource requests & limits prevent resource starvation 📈 Traffic spikes → Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales automatically 💾 Persistent storage → Volumes survive pod restarts ⏰ Scheduled retraining → CronJobs automate recurring workflows The 4 Kubernetes objects that cover most ML deployments: • Pod → Runs your container • Deployment → Manages replicas & updates • Service → Stable endpoint for your app • Ingress → Routes external traffic Flow: Ingress → Service → Deployment → Pods One lesson most tutorials skip: Always define resource requests and limits. Without them: ❌ Autoscaling becomes unreliable ❌ One workload can consume an entire node ❌ Performance becomes unpredictable And then there's Helm. Instead of managing dozens of YAML files, Helm lets you template once and deploy consistently across environments. You don't need to master Kubernetes overnight. Start with managed platforms like GKE, EKS, or AKS and focus on your ML workloads first. Caption: 📅 Dia 07 de 30 Desafio de dados Databricks Professional ✨ Managed vs. External Tables: Onde seu dado realmente mora? ​Fechando a primeira semana do desafio com chave de ouro! Hoje o foco foi entender o impacto físico e o ciclo de vida dos dados no S3/ADLS. A diferença entre uma tabela Managed e uma External vai muito além da sintaxe do código — ela define quem é o dono do dado e o que acontece quando você roda um comando fatal. ​📌 Managed Tables (Tabelas Gerenciadas) ​O conceito: O Databricks gerencia tanto os metadados no Unity Catalog quanto os arquivos físicos no cloud storage. ​O perigo: Se você executar um DROP TABLE, o Unity Catalog apaga o registro da tabela E deleta permanentemente os arquivos físicos no S3/ADLS. ​Quando usar: Ideal para tabelas onde o Databricks tem controle total do ciclo de vida (como nas camadas Silver e Gold internas). ​📌 External Tables (Tabelas Externas) ​O conceito: Você define um caminho específico via LOCATION. O Databricks passa a gerenciar apenas os metadados. ​A segurança: Se você rodar um DROP TABLE, apenas o ponteiro/registro no Unity Catalog é apagado. Os seus arquivos físicos continuam intactos no storage. ​Quando usar: Essencial quando outras ferramentas externas precisam acessar os mesmos arquivos ou quando você precisa garantir que o dado bruto jamais será deletado por acidente. ​✨ Reflexão Diária Entender o ciclo de vida físico do dado evita aquele frio na barriga clássico de sumir com Terabytes de produção por engano. Uma boa governança começa sabendo exatamente quem manda no ciclo de vida da sua infraestrutura. ​💫💻📚🌸🎯 📌 Portfólio: ericaignatios.com.br 🌸 Blog: kirabyte.com.br 📸 Instagram: 🎥 Youtube: 💻 GitHub: github.com/ericaabrantes ​estudos dados engenhariadedados databricks unitycatalog lakehouse cloudstorage pyspark

Caption: If you're chasing trends, you're already late. One of the biggest mistakes brands make in influencer marketing is believing that going viral means jumping on every trend. It doesn't. By the time a trend is identified, approved, briefed, produced, and published, the audience has often already moved on. That's why so many trend-based campaigns fail. Not because the content is bad. Not because the creators are wrong. Because the timing is. The brands that consistently generate results don't chase trends. They identify the right trends early, evaluate whether they actually fit their audience, and activate the right creators before the opportunity disappears. And there's another mistake many brands make: Assuming every viral trend is relevant to their business. A trend with millions of views means nothing if it doesn't align with your audience, your product, or your brand positioning. In influencer marketing, relevance almost always beats reach. The best-performing campaigns happen when the right trend, the right creator, and the right audience meet at the right moment. Virality isn't random. It's built. What's the biggest trend-jacking mistake you've seen brands make? Let us know in the comments. Caption: The workflow ran flawlessly for 47 days. 14,000+ successful executions. Zero issues. On day 48, at 3:42 AM, a payment gateway returned a 503 instead of a 200. Without error handling: the entire pipeline crashed silently. No Slack alert. No retry. No fallback. Nobody noticed for 72 hours. 4,200 customer invoices were never processed. The team found out from a customer complaint — not from their own monitoring. With error handling: the node retried 3 times with exponential backoff (2s, 4s, 8s). On the third failure, it triggered a fallback path that routed to a backup payment processor. Simultaneously, a Slack alert hit the on-call channel in 12 seconds. Failed records were queued in a dead letter queue for manual review. Total customer impact: zero. 5 error handling patterns every production workflow needs: 1. Retry with exponential backoff — 73% of transient API failures self-resolve within 3 attempts 2. Fallback/alternative paths — if the primary service is down, route to a backup 3. Dead letter queues — failed items go somewhere recoverable, not into the void 4. Real-time alert notifications — Slack, PagerDuty, email. Within seconds, not days 5. Graceful degradation — processing 9,800 of 10,000 records is infinitely better than processing zero Autonoly has all 5 built into the workflow builder. Every node supports retry logic, error branching, and alert triggers. No custom code required. Stop building for the happy path. Build for day 48. Caption: 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗜 𝗗𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝗔𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗛𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗔𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 "𝗩𝗶𝗯𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴" Lately, I've seen a lot of developers criticizing "vibe coding" and AI-assisted development as if it's somehow destroying software engineering. I see it differently. The problem isn't the tools. The problem is how people use them. A calculator didn't kill mathematics. GitHub didn't kill programming. Frameworks didn't kill software engineering. AI won't either. What AI does is amplify the capabilities of the person using it. If someone lacks understanding of architecture, databases, security, scalability, debugging, or software design principles, AI will simply help them make mistakes faster. But for experienced developers who understand the fundamentals, AI becomes a force multiplier. Over the last few months, I've shipped hundreds of projects ranging from SaaS platforms, digital products, business applications, web portals, mobile applications, dashboards, and desktop software. AI-assisted development didn't replace my expertise it accelerated execution. Instead of spending hours on repetitive boilerplate code, I spend more time solving business problems, improving user experiences, refining architecture, and delivering products faster. The reality is that clients don't pay for how many lines of code you write. They pay for solutions. They pay for products that work. They pay for results. The developers who will thrive in the coming years won't be the ones fighting AI. They'll be the ones learning how to combine technical expertise, product thinking, and AI tools to build better software faster than ever before. AI is not replacing developers. Developers who know how to leverage AI effectively are replacing those who refuse to adapt. What's your take on AI-assisted development and vibe coding? Caption: Begint je AI-agent vaker fouten te maken? Dan denk je misschien dat prompt engineering de oplossing is. Maar het probleem zit eigenlijk ergens anders: Er is een vaardigheid die veel meer impact heeft en waar nog weinig over gesproken wordt, namelijk context engineering. De twee klinken gelijkaardig, maar ze spelen zich op een heel ander niveau af. ➡ Prompt engineering gaat alleen over hoe je je prompt opstelt. ➡ Context engineering gaat over alles wat een AI-agent weet gedurende een volledige werksessie, en hoe je dat actief beheert. Moderne AI-modellen hebben een context window van zo'n 200.000 tokens. Dat klinkt ruim, tot je ziet hoe snel die volloopt. Een agent die tegelijk je codebase analyseert, tools aanroept, gesprekshistoriek bijhoudt en instructies onthoudt, vult die ruimte sneller dan je denkt. Veel developers zullen het gevoel herkennen. Je werkt al een tijdje met je agent, en code die hij een halfuur geleden nog correct schreef, zit nu vol fouten. Hij lijkt de instructies te vergeten die je aan het begin van de sessie meegaf. Dus pas je je prompt aan, maar het wordt er niet beter op. Het voelt alsof de tool gewoon onbetrouwbaar is, maar eigenlijk zit de context window gewoon te vol om nog goed te kunnen redeneren. Er is een drempel, ruwweg 40% van de context window, waarna de kwaliteit merkbaar daalt. Ontwikkelaars noemen dat de "Dumb Zone". De meeste mensen weten niet dat die drempel bestaat, en werken er daardoor de hele tijd tegenaan zonder te begrijpen wat er misgaat. De oplossing zit in begrijpen wat er in die context window zit, wat eruit moet, en hoe je een agent structureert zodat hij gefocust blijft. Een andere prompt schrijven lost het probleem niet op. Caption: Your AI has six doors into your business. Most companies have only ever locked the front one. When most people think about AI security, they think about keeping attackers out. Firewalls. Authentication. Access controls. The front door. But AI systems don't operate through a single door. They interact with users, consume data, connect to tools, store context, integrate with third-party systems, and influence business processes. Each of those becomes a potential entry point. Here are six doors every organization should be paying attention to: 1. The Prompt Door Anyone who can interact with your AI can attempt to influence its behavior. 2. The Data Door AI systems learn from and rely on the information they receive. Poor or manipulated data can create poor outcomes. 3. The Tool Door Every API, database, email platform, or business system connected to AI expands its ability to take action. 4. The Memory Door What your AI remembers can be just as important as what it knows. Retained context creates both value and risk. 5. The Integration Door Third-party applications, plugins, and connectors often introduce risks organizations never evaluate. 6. The Human Door Employees remain one of the largest attack surfaces. Shadow AI usage, unmanaged tools, and poor practices can bypass even the strongest technical controls. The mistake many organizations make is securing the model while ignoring the ecosystem around it. But attackers rarely target the strongest point They look for the easiest door. The question isn't: "Is our AI secure?" The better question is: "Which of these six doors is currently open?" Because AI security isn't about protecting a model. It's about securing every pathway that can influence its decisions and actions. 📌 Save this post and use it as a checklist during your next AI security review. Caption: These are 9 DevOps mistakes that show up repeatedly in startups. Some are expensive. Some are embarrassing. A few can take down entire systems. 1. One AWS account for everything Dev, staging, and production in the same account creates unnecessary risk. A dev misconfiguration can directly impact production or cost. Separate accounts early. 2. No billing alerts Without cost monitoring, cloud spend becomes invisible until it’s too late. A single Auto Scaling misconfiguration once triggered 50 instances instead of 5 for days. Result: a $12,000 bill. 3. Over-engineering before launch Kubernetes, service meshes, and complex infrastructure before product-market fit. Most early-stage systems fail from complexity, not lack of scale. 4. Hardcoded AWS credentials Embedding credentials in code or repositories is a critical security risk. Secrets should be managed properly from day one (not “later”). 5. Public SSH access (0.0.0.0/0 on port 22) Exposing SSH to the internet guarantees exposure to automated brute-force attacks. Session Manager or restricted access should be the default. 6. Deploying on Friday afternoons Production changes close to weekends increase risk and slow response time if something breaks. Deployment timing is part of reliability strategy. 7. No rollback strategy Every deployment should answer one question: How is this reverted in minutes if it breaks production? Without that, deployments are high-risk events. 8. No monitoring before launch Monitoring after an outage is reactive, not operational maturity. CloudWatch alarms and health checks should exist before production traffic. 9. Single point of failure everywhere Single EC2, single AZ, single NAT Gateway introduces avoidable downtime risk. Systems should assume components will fail not behave perfectly. Most production incidents are not caused by complex failures. They come from basic infrastructure decisions made too early or too casually. Strong DevOps practice is often just avoiding these fundamentals. devops aws cloudcomputing sre systemdesign

Caption: Patch day. Two words that can trigger anything from mild annoyance to full-blown panic depending on how old your infrastructure is. Most teams don't intentionally neglect updates. They're busy shipping features, onboarding customers and fixing production issues. Updating third-party infrastructure components often ends up somewhere at the bottom of the backlog, right next to all those things everyone agrees are important but nobody has time for. The problem is that technical debt compounds. Maybe your Kubernetes version is a few releases behind. Your Helm charts haven't been updated in months. That Terraform provider still works alright, so why check it? Then eventually the day comes when you actually need to upgrade something and suddenly you're not upgrading one version. You're upgrading ten or more. I've seen this happen more than once. What should have been a routine maintenance task turned into a project spanning several weeks because too many dependencies had drifted too far apart. The longer you delay, the more painful it becomes. That's why I'm a big fan of continuous upgrades. Not because upgrading software is exciting. It isn't. But reviewing ten small changes every week is significantly easier than reviewing three hundred changes once per year. Tools like Renovate help automate a large part of that process. Instead of manually checking every dependency, container image, Terraform provider or Helm chart, Renovate continuously scans for updates and creates pull requests automatically. You still stay in control. Nothing gets deployed without review, but your team no longer has to remember what needs updating and when. The result is usually not only just better security, but also less operational risk. Because patch days stop being special events. They become part of normal operations. How are you currently handling updates for third-party infrastructure components? Are you already using Renovate or are upgrades still mostly manual? Caption: ⚡ Most data engineers use Spark every day — but freeze when asked: "What does the Driver actually do?" Here's the truth nobody told you clearly: Spark has a "Brain" and a "Muscle." 🧠 DRIVER = The Brain → Converts your code into a DAG (execution plan) → Schedules tasks across the cluster → Tracks which executor is alive and which crashed → Never processes a single row of data itself 💪 EXECUTOR = The Muscle → Actually runs your transformations & actions → Caches data in memory for speed → Sends heartbeats to the Driver every few seconds → Lives on worker nodes across the cluster Here's what nobody talks about: If your Driver dies → your entire job dies. It holds the SparkContext. If one Executor dies → Spark just reruns that task elsewhere. No drama. Knowing this one thing changes how you debug, tune, and architect every Spark application you'll ever write. Caption: 📅 Dia 08 de 30 do Desafio de dados Databricks Professional ✨ Auto Loader Master: Schema Evolution e Detecção de Drift ​Abrindo a segunda semana do desafio com o pé no acelerador em Ingestão Escalável e Streaming! Hoje o foco total foi dominar o Auto Loader e aprender a lidar com uma das maiores dores de cabeça na engenharia de dados: a mudança repentina na estrutura dos arquivos que chegam no Data Lake. ​📌 O Poder do Auto Loader (cloudFiles) ​Ingestão Incremental Eficiente: Ele descobre novos arquivos assim que eles chegam no S3/ADLS de forma absurdamente eficiente, usando notificação de arquivos ou listagem otimizada, sem precisar reprocessar o que já passou. ​Schema Evolution (Evolução de Esquema): Em vez de o pipeline quebrar no meio da madrugada porque uma nova coluna surgiu, o Auto Loader consegue detectar a mudança e evoluir o schema automaticamente (cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode), adaptando a tabela Delta sem intervenção manual. ​Detecção de Schema Drift com _rescued_data: Se uma coluna nova aparecer ou um tipo de dado mudar drasticamente, o Auto Loader joga essa informação para uma coluna especial de "dados resgatados". Isso garante que o pipeline continue rodando e nenhum dado seja perdido enquanto você analisa a mudança. ​✨ Reflexão Diária No mundo real, os dados são vivos e mudam o tempo todo. Um pipeline verdadeiramente resiliente não é aquele que assume que o dado sempre virá perfeito, mas sim aquele que sabe se adaptar ao "drift" de forma inteligente e segura. Caption: Why the data system your company built for basic reporting is quietly failing your AI. 🛑🖥️ Most corporations organize their modern data lakes using a pattern called the "Medallion Architecture," which filters raw info through three separate steps (Bronze, Silver, and Gold). While this is great for basic charts and graphs, it creates a massive blind spot for advanced AI features like search bots and automated assistants. When an AI model hallucinated or retrieves the wrong document piece, your developers need to know exactly where and when that individual row of data was corrupted. Traditional systems can only track large groups of tables, making finding a single broken record look like searching for a needle in a haystack. Upgrading to Apache Iceberg v3 introduces native Row Lineage. This smart update tags every single row with its own digital passport (_row_id), allowing your engineers to instantly query the life history of any data record with 100% precision. Stop trying to power tomorrow's AI on yesterday's blueprints. Learn how to architect elite, crystal-clear enterprise data platforms at DataEngineering ApacheIceberg DataOps

Caption: CASE STUDY: ONLINE COACH 📈 An online coach had a problem many businesses secretly struggle with. People were visiting her website every day. Traffic wasn't the issue. The real question was: **"If people are visiting my website, why aren't they buying?"** Hundreds of visitors would come. They would read about her programs. Browse her services. Then leave. No enquiry. No purchase. No follow-up. Then she realized something important: **Most people don't buy the first time they see your offer.** People need time. People need trust. People need reminders. So instead of trying to sell immediately, she changed her strategy. She created a simple **5-day email nurture sequence.** For five days, she stayed connected with her audience. 📩 Day 1: Welcome email and her story 📩 Day 2: Valuable tips and practical advice 📩 Day 3: Client success stories and testimonials 📩 Day 4: Solutions to common objections 📩 Day 5: A clear offer with a call to action She stopped chasing customers. She started building relationships. The results after just 30 days were impressive: 📧 48% email open rate 📈 27% increase in sales The biggest lesson? 💡 **Follow-up creates conversions.** Many businesses lose customers not because their product is bad, but because they stop the conversation too early. Remember this: ❌ Website visitors are not lost opportunities. ❌ People rarely buy the first time they see you. ✅ Consistent follow-up builds trust. ✅ Trust creates sales. The fortune is often in the follow-up. 👇 Be honest: Are you following up with your potential customers? Caption: The game changed. The foundation didn't. Search used to be about ranking on Google. Now it's about being trusted by AI. But here's what most marketers are getting wrong: they're treating GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation) and SEO as a choice — pick one, skip the other. That's not how it works. → GEO without SEO means AI has no reason to trust you. No domain authority, no structured content, no backlink credibility — AI models skip right past you when forming answers. → SEO without GEO means you rank on Google, but you're invisible when someone asks ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Gemini a question your business should be answering. You don't get to choose one layer. Both need to run simultaneously, or you're already losing ground to competitors who figured this out. The brands winning in AI-era search built their SEO foundation first — then layered GEO on top: structured answers, cited content, E-E-A-T signals, semantic clarity. The question isn't SEO or GEO. Caption: Hey fam! Last night, we joined AI Tinkerers Hong Kong & GBA at Dialogue in the Dark, a great evening about building AI that genuinely enables. 🤖 The night opened the way it should: with the people AI is meant to serve. Visually impaired hosts from Dialogue in the Dark shared how AI is already reshaping their daily lives and, just as importantly, the real-world UX problems they still need engineers to solve. A grounding reminder that accessibility isn’t a feature you bolt on at the end; it’s the brief. 🙂 From there, the demos. Three teams shared technical work spanning two accessibility projects and a live translation app - the kind of “does it actually work in the wild?” building we love to see. AWS & Kiro also dropped in for a session (and kept the room fed 🙏). What struck us most was the crowd: deeply technical, hands-on, the kind of people training their own models and hacking on hard problems for the right reasons. Exactly the energy we really love being around! 😉 At OAX Foundation, this is the intersection we care about: AI that extends human capability and reaches the people who need it most. It’s also why we back projects like mapping the people, ideas, and events moving Asia’s AI scene forward. Nights like this are a big part of that story. 🥰 Huge thanks to Dialogue in the Dark for hosting, and to AI Tinkerers HK & GBA for convening such a thoughtful room. More of this, please! 🥂 tech startup hongkong

Caption: You know when you type a question into your LLM (let's say Claude), and it says...thinking... Or, it gives you the impression it's thinking. Well, it's not. Your AI is a predication engine. It doesn't have thoughts, or feelings for that matter. It has lots and lots of data and it uses that to predict the most likely answer. This means, it doesn't always get it right, which is why fact checking is so important. Being honest, have you started to rely on AI a bit like it's a friend? Seriously no judgement! 😊 It's easy to do, that's what tech companies are trying to achieve in their interfaces and responses. Try this instead. Use your LLM to help challenge you. To broaden your cognitive skills, not lessen them. Try sparring with your AI model on a subject you know about and whilst doing so, remember, it's a prediction engine, it's not really thinking and you can't hurt its feelings. Caption: AI can do a lot, but it can't carry responsibility for your decisions. That's why the smartest teams are building AI and human judgement side by side, on purpose. AI is great at the heavy lifting: analysing data, spotting patterns, and drafting options in seconds. Humans are great at the trust work: nuance, empathy, ethical reasoning, and accountability. So before you roll out another tool, get clear on roles. What will AI automate, what will it advise on, and what must a person approve every time? Next, build a workflow where AI outputs come with a review moment, not an auto-send button. If the decision affects people, money, safety, or privacy, add stronger oversight and clear escalation paths. Keep the loop tight so your AI improves responsibly: create, deploy, measure, review, refine, redeploy. And reinvest the time you save into the skills that compound, like critical thinking, communication, and great leadership. Caption: The Startup DevOps Checklist. Not for reading once. For reviewing monthly. Because most outages don’t come from unknown problems, they come from skipped basics. Foundation ↳ Root account MFA enabled ↳ CloudTrail enabled across all regions ↳ Billing alerts set (50%, 80%, 100%) ↳ Separate AWS accounts for dev / staging / prod ↳ Infrastructure managed as code (Terraform only) ↳ Remote state stored in S3 with DynamoDB locking / S3 native lock ↳ Pre-commit hooks enabled (no exposed secrets in git) Security ↳ No production IAM users with AdministratorAccess ↳ All secrets stored in Secrets Manager / Parameter Store ↳ No public exposure of ports (except 80/443) ↳ RDS deployed in private subnets only ↳ GuardDuty enabled across all regions ↳ Container/image scanning in CI/CD (e.g., Trivy) Pipeline ↳ CI/CD triggered on every commit to main ↳ Stages include: lint → test → build → scan → deploy ↳ Images tagged with commit SHA (never “latest”) ↳ Rollback procedure documented and tested ↳ No manual production deployments ↳ Deployment freeze after Friday 12pm Operations ↳ CloudWatch alarms for CPU, memory, errors, latency ↳ Auto Scaling Group health checks configured properly ↳ Application health checks in boot/user data flows ↳ Log retention policies defined ↳ Runbooks exist for top failure scenarios ↳ Postmortem process defined and ready Most production incidents are not caused by missing advanced tools. They are caused by missing basics that were never enforced. How many of these are currently in place? The gaps are usually not theoretical. They are where the next incident will come from. devops aws cloudcomputing sre systemdesign

Caption: Your dashboard's 7-day average has been a running total this whole time. Write avg(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day) with no frame and Postgres defaults to RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING — it averages every row from the start, not a sliding window. Your "moving average" slowly flattens into a cumulative total and quietly understates every recent trend. The fix is one clause: ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW pins a fixed 7-row window for a true moving average. Same trap applies to SUM, MIN and MAX — always state the frame. Caption: The hidden cost of "it works on my local machine" usually shows up as an expensive cloud bill in production. 💸 When you are joining tables in Apache Spark, how often do you actually check how Spark is handling it? If your answer is "never," your data pipelines are likely suffering from severe network bottlenecks. Let's demystify Spark's two primary join strategies: 1️⃣ Broadcast Hash Join (BHJ): The ultimate cheat code. If one of your dataframes is small (under 10MB by default), Spark duplicates it across all worker nodes. Zero shuffling over the network. It's blindingly fast, but try it on a large dataset and you’ll instantly trigger an OOM error. 💥 2️⃣ Sort Merge Join (SMJ): The reliable workhorse. When dealing with two massive datasets, Spark shuffles, sorts, and merges them. It's slower because moving data across network nodes takes time, but it handles massive scale without breaking a sweat. 🏋️‍♂️ The magic happens when you know how to configure spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold or use explicit broadcast hints in your code to turn a sluggish pipeline into a high-performance engine. Caption: 𝗦𝘁𝗲𝗽𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗮𝗻 𝗠𝗩𝗣 🚀 Many startups fail because they try to build a perfect product before validating the idea. An MVP (Minimum Viable Product) is not about building everything. It’s about building the smallest version of a product that solves a real problem and gets real user feedback. Here’s the process I follow when delivering an MVP: ✅ 1. Understand the Problem Before writing a single line of code, understand the user’s pain points, business goals, and target audience. ✅ 2. Define Core Features List all features and identify the 20% that deliver 80% of the value. Everything else can wait. ✅ 3. Create Wireframes & User Flow Map out how users will interact with the product. A clear user journey saves countless development hours. ✅ 4. Design the UI/UX Create a simple, clean, and intuitive interface. MVPs don’t need fancy animations—they need usability. ✅ 5. Build the Database Structure A well-planned database prevents major issues when scaling later. ✅ 6. Develop Core Functionality Focus only on the features required for launch. Avoid feature creep. ✅ 7. Testing & Debugging Test every workflow, edge case, and user action. Reliability matters more than having extra features. ✅ 8. Launch Quickly Get the product into the hands of real users as soon as possible. ✅ 9. Collect Feedback Listen to users, analyze behavior, and identify what needs improvement. ✅ 10. Iterate & Scale Use real feedback to build the next version instead of making assumptions. ➡️ The goal of an MVP is not perfection. ➡️ The goal is learning. ➡️ Build fast. ➡️ Launch early. ➡️ Learn quickly. ➡️ Improve continuously. ✅ That’s how successful products are created. Caption: 🔐 **Why is Anti-Money Laundering (AML) the first line of defense in today's financial landscape?** Financial crimes are becoming increasingly sophisticated, making traditional monitoring no longer enough. Money laundering often follows recognizable patterns, including: • Structuring – splitting large transactions to avoid reporting thresholds. • Layering – moving funds across multiple accounts to obscure their origin. • Integration – reintroducing illicit funds into the legitimate economy. • Shell Companies – using business entities to disguise ownership and transactions. • Cash-Out – quickly withdrawing and transferring funds to erase digital traces. To combat these evolving threats, organizations need an AML solution that goes beyond rule-based detection. Modern AML platforms should provide: ✅ Real-time cross-reference ✅ Network analysis ✅ Real-time risk scoring ✅ Pattern recognition ✅ Automated reporting to regulatory authorities The future of financial security starts with the right infrastructure. AI-powered AML solutions help financial institutions detect suspicious activities faster, reduce false positives, and stay compliant in an increasingly complex regulatory environment. Caption: Tax season may never feel the same again 🤖📄 For many Italians, taxes mean stress, missing receipts, and the fear of forgetting a deduction. But behind the scenes, AI is quietly changing the way accountants work. Instead of spending hours on manual data entry, accountants can now use AI tools with advanced OCR and machine learning to read, organize, and interpret documents faster. The real shift? AI is not here to replace professionals. It can help free them from repetitive tasks so they can become more strategic advisors. Here’s what this could mean for taxpayers: ✅ Fewer human oversights by cross-checking invoices, medical expenses, transfers, and other documents ⚡ Faster processing, turning tasks that once took days into hours 💡 More personalized advice, helping identify tax relief opportunities that might otherwise be missed But there’s a big “if.” AI in tax work must be handled with privacy, security, and human judgment at the center. Sensitive financial data needs strong protection. And because AI can sometimes produce confident but incorrect answers, accountants still need to review, interpret, and take responsibility for the final decisions. For citizens and small businesses, the takeaway is practical: 📌 Ask your accountant what digital tools they use and how your data is protected 📌 Keep documents organized in clean digital formats like PDF or XML 📌 Use the time saved on bureaucracy to talk about planning, strategy, and smarter financial decisions AI could help make tax season less painful and more transparent, but only if humans stay in control of ethics, context, and critical thinking. Would you trust AI to help manage your tax documents if a human expert still reviewed everything? Caption: **Most SaaS founders chase ads.** **This founder chased accountants.** When **Srijan Singh** joined his family's deep-tech business, he expected to learn about industrial automation. Instead, he found something surprising. The machines were running perfectly. **The accounting wasn't.** As businesses expanded across multiple locations and compliance became more complex, accounting teams were still spending hours closing books, fixing manual entries and adapting themselves to software that wasn't built for how Indian accountants actually work. Legacy software had become outdated. New-age accounting apps looked modern... ...but many still forced accountants to change their workflow instead of supporting it. Srijan saw an opportunity. That insight became **Kitaabh**—an accounting platform designed around the realities of Indian accounting rather than generic global workflows. But here's what makes the story interesting. He didn't launch expensive marketing campaigns. He didn't spend heavily on paid ads. Instead, he carried the product to **CA conferences and accounting expos.** He sat beside chartered accountants. Watched them use the software. Noticed exactly where they struggled. Improved the product. Then repeated the process again. Every conversation became product research. Every demo became customer validation. ### Why this matters: Many founders try to scale before deeply understanding their users. Srijan did the opposite. He spent less time chasing impressions... ...and more time removing friction. Sometimes the fastest way to grow isn't finding more customers. It's understanding the ones already sitting in front of you. **Question:** If you were building a B2B SaaS startup today, would you spend your first ₹10 lakh on digital marketing—or on meeting 1,000 customers face-to-face? Caption: AI agents can write code, analyze data, and trade crypto. But they've never been able to do something far simpler: pay for things on their own. Every time an agent wants to call a paid API or query a premium data feed, a human has to step in. Sign up. Generate an API key. Click approve. Project-r0x changes that. It's an open-source toolkit that lets AI agents discover, pay for, and use online services autonomously. Built on Robinhood Chain using USDG stablecoin, it's powered by the x402 protocol — a revival of HTTP 402 "Payment Required." No API keys. No accounts. No human approval. Through the MCP plugin for Claude Code, agents get 18 tools for trading, yield, bridging, and liquidity management. Every paid skill costs a flat $0.01 USDG. The project is early-stage with real tradeoffs, but it represents something genuinely new: a working implementation of agent-to-service payments without human intermediation. If this vision plays out, API keys might one day look as outdated as dial-up modems. Proper classification, governance, encryption, and compliance help protect sensitive information, maintain customer trust, and satisfy legal and regulatory requirements. Key concepts: 🔹 Data Classification Not all data requires the same level of protection. Organizations classify data based on its sensitivity, such as: Public – Safe to share openly Internal – Intended for organizational use only Confidential – Highly sensitive information requiring strict access controls Proper classification helps determine the appropriate security measures, monitoring, and access policies. 🔹 Data Governance Data governance ensures that sensitive information is: Properly protected throughout its lifecycle Accessible only to authorized users Monitored and audited continuously Managed according to organizational policies and legal requirements 🔹 Compliance Standards AWS provides services and controls that help organizations meet industry regulations, including: • PCI DSS – Protects payment card information through encryption, logging, and strong access controls. • HIPAA – Safeguards healthcare and patient information by enforcing confidentiality, encryption, and auditing. • GDPR – Protects personal data of EU citizens through privacy controls, consent management, and data protection requirements. 🔹 AWS Security Services AWS supports data protection using services such as: Amazon S3 Amazon EBS Amazon RDS Amazon DynamoDB AWS Key Management Service (KMS) AWS CloudHSM IAM AWS CloudTrail Amazon CloudWatch These services help secure data through encryption, key management, access control, monitoring, backups, and auditing. Caption: Don't Just Monitor Data. Monitor the Right Metric. Setting up alerts is easy. Setting up meaningful alerts is what makes a monitoring system effective. In Databricks SQL Alerts, you can monitor aggregated metrics instead of individual records. This allows you to detect trends and anomalies that matter, rather than reacting to every data point. For example, if you're monitoring sensor data, you can calculate the average temperature for each sensor and trigger an alert only when the average exceeds a threshold for multiple consecutive executions. This approach helps you: ✔️ Reduce false alarms caused by temporary spikes ✔️ Focus on sustained issues instead of one-off events ✔️ Improve the reliability of operational monitoring ✔️ Receive notifications only when action is actually needed By combining aggregations, thresholds, and consecutive alert conditions, you can build monitoring systems that are both accurate and practical for production environments. 💡 Key Takeaway Effective monitoring isn't about generating more alerts—it's about generating the right alerts. Designing alerts around aggregated metrics and consecutive evaluations helps surface real issues while reducing unnecessary noise. Caption: Batch reCAPTCHA form submissions need more than just solving tokens. When you are processing multiple forms, solving one token at a time can slow the entire workflow. A better approach is to use a token pipeline: solve tokens in the background, keep a small fresh buffer, and submit forms as tokens become available. But token freshness matters. reCAPTCHA tokens are short-lived and should be used quickly. If your buffer is too large, tokens may expire before submission. If it is too small, your form pipeline may stall while waiting for new tokens. A reliable pipeline should include: • Fresh token queue • Small buffer size • One token per form submission • Token age checks • Separate pools for different sitekeys • Session and IP consistency • Monitoring for expired or rejected tokens The goal is not to stockpile tokens. The goal is to deliver the right fresh token to the right form at the right time. This type of workflow should only be used in owned, client-authorized, or contractually permitted environments. automationengineering Recaptcha CaptchaAI PythonAutomation DevOps APIMonitoring WorkflowAutomation DataEngineering FormAutomation EngineeringTips

Caption: Data doesn’t move itself. Here’s what a data pipeline actually is, minus the jargon. A pipeline moves data from source to useful, on a schedule, again and again. Every number you trust rode one to get there. It runs in four stages: ingest, store, transform, serve. Ingest pulls data out of every source, APIs, databases, event streams, files, using tools like Fivetran, Airbyte, or Kafka. Transform turns raw into trustworthy: clean, dedupe, join, model, usually with dbt or Spark. (Transform before loading is ETL; after is ELT.) Then something has to run it on time, so Airflow, Dagster, or Prefect schedule the steps as a DAG and shout when one fails. That scheduling is the real job. The 9am fire drill you’ll recognize: “why is the dashboard showing yesterday’s numbers?” Nine times out of ten a pipeline broke upstream, a source changed or a job died quietly at 2am. That’s why monitoring matters, and why good pipelines are boring: they run on time, fail loudly, and never make you doubt the numbers. What’s your pipeline stack, Airflow, Dagster, or something else? Caption: Why AI models need billions of parameters. You hear terms like '70-billion parameter model' constantly. But what actually is a parameter? In neural networks, parameters are the mathematical knobs (weights and biases) that determine how signals propagate. Here is why models require billions of parameters to operate: 🎛️ Static Rules vs. Knobs: Traditional software uses hand-coded if/else rules, which break under language complexity. Neural networks replace rules with parameters: dynamic float values adjusting variables automatically. 🧮 Weights & Biases: Every parameter is either a Weight (w) scaling input signal strengths, or a Bias (b) shifting output thresholds, forming the linear equation y = wx + b at each node. 📈 Scaling the Complexity Wall: Mapping a line requires 2 parameters. Mapping the English language (grammar, coding logic, facts, tone, sarcasm) requires billions of parameter slots to hold conceptual connections. 📚 Deep Layer Abstractions: Parameters are stacked. Shallow layers map basic structures like letters. Middle layers track grammar. Deep layers map logical reasoning and complex programming syntax. 🔧 Tuning Billions of Knobs: During training, backpropagation compares guesses to target text, updating weights by tiny fractions using gradients to minimize errors. Caption: Micro vs. macro influencers: which one actually pays off? 👇 Everyone chases follower count. But engagement — not audience size — is what drives ROI. 🔹 Micro-influencers (10K–100K): ~6% engagement, $250–$1.5K per post, ~$0.05 per engaged follower. Small, trusting, niche audiences. 🔹 Macro-influencers (1M+): ~1.5% engagement, $10K–$100K+ per post, $1–$2 per engaged follower. Big reach, lower intimacy. Same $25K budget → 50 micro-influencers can out-deliver 1 macro-influencer on engaged reach. The move: use macro for awareness, micro for trust and conversions. Most brands need both — just not in equal measure. Which one is your brand leaning on right now? Tell us below 👇 Follow for more no-fluff marketing breakdowns. Caption: Most deals don't die because of price. They die because trust disappears. Recently, I came across a simple framework in Ryan Serhant's Sell It Like Serhant that reinforced something I've experienced throughout my career in B2B sales, SaaS, AI, and enterprise technology. The principles are timeless because they reflect how people make buying decisions. Here are six reasons deals quietly fall apart: You fail to communicate clearly. You react instead of responding with intention. You create expectations your team can't deliver. You don't understand your customer's business deeply enough. Your approach has become stale and predictable. You're more focused on your commission than on your customer's outcome. Notice something? None of these have anything to do with price. Or discounts. Or "closing techniques." Sales is rarely won by the person who talks the most. It's won by the person who creates the most certainty. Reading Sell It Like Serhant reminded me that while technology keeps evolving, the fundamentals of great selling don't. That's one of the ideas behind BoringSales. AI can help you scale. Automation can help you move faster. But neither replaces trust, curiosity, preparation, or genuine expertise. The best sales professionals don't convince people to buy. They remove the reasons not to buy. I'd love to hear your perspective. Which of these six deal killers do you encounter most often? 1️⃣ Poor communication 2️⃣ Unrealistic expectations 3️⃣ Lack of product or industry knowledge 4️⃣ Generic sales approach 5️⃣ Being too focused on the money 6️⃣ Something else? Share your answer in the comments. Let's compare notes.

Caption: The simplest architecture consists of a single agent. One agent receives the user's request, determines what actions are required, calls the necessary tools, retrieves information when appropriate, and generates a response. For many business applications, this architecture is entirely sufficient. Customer support. Knowledge assistants. Internal search. Document summarization. Simple workflow automation. These applications often benefit from a single well-designed agent rather than a collection of specialized agents. Simplicity is frequently the most effective optimization strategy. As AI applications become more sophisticated, organizations often divide responsibilities among multiple specialized agents. One agent performs research. Another retrieves documents. Another analyzes financial information. Another writes reports. Another validates outputs. Another reviews compliance requirements. Specialization frequently improves maintainability and allows different models or prompts to be optimized for different tasks. However, specialization also introduces additional infrastructure. Every agent requires reasoning. Every interaction between agents generates additional inference. Messages must be exchanged. Context must be transferred. Memory must be synchronized. The architecture becomes increasingly distributed. Cloud costs increase accordingly. The question therefore should never be how many agents can be deployed. Caption: 2026년 220번째 서적 🙋‍♂”여전히 부동의 1위 AWS”’ _ 클라우드 시장(Iaas)의 부동의 1위는 AWS(아마존 웹 서비스)입니다. 올해 6월기준 전세계 시장 점유율 38%정도를 유지하고 있고 그 다음이 마이크로소프트의 Azure입니다. 세번째가 구글 클라우드가 될 것이니 클라우드 서비스를 이해한다는 것은 적어도 구글 클라우드 이상부터 학습을 해야한다는 것을 의미합니다. 실제 데이터 시각화의 경우 세일즈포스의 태블로와 MS의 Power BI가 양분하는 것처럼 클라우드 서비스와 유관 인프라 학습은 아마존의 AWS를 학습해야 하며, 관련 인프라에 대한 관심으로 를 읽어보게 되었습니다. AWS는 클라우드 컴퓨팅 서비스입니다. 해당 서비스는 실제 기능은 유사할 수 있으나 UI나 UX 그리고 접근방식과 디테일에서 각사별 차이가 존재합니다. 본서는 클라우드 컴퓨팅의 개념부터 계정가입(Free Tier)부터 보안설정, 그리고 가성서버의 운영 플랫폼인 EC2와 IAM와 네트워킹 서비스를 비롯하여 권한 및 보안관리까지 서적의 제목그래도 AWS의 기본적인 구조부터 활용방법까지를 다루고 있습니다. 비관련자분들에게는 본서의 내용이 상당히 딱딱할 수 있어서 친절한 서적은 아니라고 생각합니다. 그래서 본서는 입에 쓴 좋은 약에 가깝습니다. 다만 클라우드 인프라와 유관업계에서 AWS관련 자격증 보유나 AWS를 통해 본인의 포트폴리오에 유의미한 경력을 넣는 것은 조금 다른 차원의 이슈입니다. 예를 들어 대형 클라우드 사업자가 아니더라도, 개인이 app을 만들고 운영할때 많은 트래픽과 스토리지, 데이터 사용량이 있어서 AWS를 사용하고 관련 확장을 해보았다면 이는 개인적으로도 도움이되고, 실무경험으로도 도움이 되는 부분입니다. 제가 본서를 읽은 것은 현업과 관련된 내역과 개인적은 활용때문이고 본서는 최신의 AWS내용과 콘솔까지를 잘 반영한 부분이라 앞으로도 발췌독하면서 유용한 부분을 이용할 계획입니다. ’글로벌 표준‘ 📖AWS교과서 ✒김원일 📍길벗 AWS 아키텍쳐

Caption: Think df.dropDuplicates() is saving your PySpark pipeline? Think again. ❌ When an interviewer asks you to handle duplicate records based on specific criteria—like keeping the most recent order or the highest transaction amount—using dropDuplicates() on a subset of columns is a massive red flag. 🚩 Because Apache Spark is a distributed framework, rows are shuffled and processed across multiple cluster nodes. Without explicit sorting, dropDuplicates() picks a row non-deterministically. You have zero control over which record stays and which one gets thrown away. It might work on a tiny mockup dataset, but it will corrupt your data at scale. To pass the senior data engineer test, you must use a Window specification (Window.partitionBy().orderBy()) paired with row_number(). This approach lets you cleanly isolate the exact record you need, making your code bulletproof and deterministic. Caption: Exploring Kafka's Internal Architecture: Delivering Scalable, Fault-Tolerant Messaging Apache Kafka has become the backbone of modern real-time data platforms, enabling organizations to process millions of events reliably and efficiently. Here are the key building blocks behind Kafka's architecture: Topics & Partitions: Organize and distribute data for parallel processing and horizontal scalability. Producers & Consumers: Producers publish events, while consumers process them independently, enabling decoupled system design. Brokers & Clusters: Multiple brokers work together to provide high availability, scalability, and fault tolerance. Replication: Data is replicated across brokers, ensuring durability and minimizing data loss during failures. Event Streaming: Power real-time analytics, IoT, fraud detection, logging, and microservices with continuous event processing. Kafka Connect & Kafka Streams: Simplify data integration and enable real-time stream processing with minimal effort. Kafka's distributed architecture, durability, and high throughput make it a preferred platform for building resilient, event-driven applications at scale. Where have you used Kafka, log aggregation, event streaming, microservices, or real-time analytics? Share your experience! Caption: "Mon site est sur Google." D'accord. Mais sur quelle page ? Parce qu'être sur Google et être VU sur Google, ce sont deux mondes différents. La page 2 de Google, c'est le meilleur endroit pour cacher un corps. Personne n'y va jamais. Voici un auto-diagnostic gratuit. 5 symptômes. Coche mentalement les tiens. → Tu apparais sur Google, mais jamais en première page. → Tu as du trafic, mais il ne se transforme pas en demandes. → Tes pages n'ont pas de titres ni de descriptions travaillés. → Tes concurrents te passent devant sur les mêmes recherches. → Tu sens que ton site pourrait ressortir bien plus haut. Un ou deux symptômes ? Rien de grave, tu ajustes. Trois ou plus ? Tu laisses des places (et des clients) en haut de Google. Le plus important : tu peux commencer à corriger ce soir, seul. Ta première action, la plus rentable : 1. Ouvre ton site. 2. Regarde l'onglet de ton navigateur (l'onglet en haut). Le texte qui s'affiche, c'est ton "titre" (title). Le résumé sous ton lien dans Google, c'est ta "description". 3. Pose-toi une seule question : est-ce qu'ils donnent envie de cliquer ET est-ce qu'ils contiennent le mot que ton client tape ? Exemple concret. Mauvais : "Accueil" Bon : "Plombier à Cotonou - Dépannage rapide 7j/7" Le premier ne dit rien à Google ni au client. Le second dit exactement qui tu es, ce que tu fais, où. Google adore. Le client clique. Fais ça sur tes 5 pages principales cette semaine. C'est gratuit. Ça bouge déjà les lignes. Un site bien réglé, ce n'est pas une dépense. Caption: More autonomy isn't the flex. Bounded autonomy is. The hard part of an AI agent was never the model. It's the boundaries you put around it. Think of an agent as a capable junior with perfect patience and zero institutional knowledge. It'll follow a process tirelessly — but it needs to be told exactly what it can and can't do on its own. The four things that actually make an agent production-ready (none of them are the AI): - Least-privilege access — if it CAN delete records, one day it will - Approval gates — a human signs off before anything costly - Audit logging — every action traceable - A named owner — because workflows drift The agents that blow up in production usually weren't dumb. They were over-permissioned, with no gate and no log. Start with one small lane. Prove it. Then widen it. Save this for your next AI project. . . . Caption: 🖥️ 서버를 이해하면 IT 인프라가 보입니다! 🌐 우리가 매일 사용하는 웹사이트, 이메일, 인터넷, 클라우드 서비스는 모두 다양한 서버(Server) 가 협력하여 동작합니다. 서버는 단순한 컴퓨터가 아니라, 각자의 전문 역할을 수행하며 기업의 IT 서비스를 안정적으로 운영하는 핵심 시스템입니다. 이번 인포그래픽에서는 네트워크와 시스템 관리자가 반드시 알아야 할 8가지 핵심 서버 종류와 역할을 한눈에 정리했습니다. ⸻ 🚀 꼭 알아야 할 8가지 핵심 서버 🌐 ① Web Server (웹 서버) * 웹사이트와 웹 애플리케이션 제공 * HTTP/HTTPS 요청 처리 * Apache, Nginx, IIS, PHP, Node.js 등 지원 * SSL/TLS 기반 암호화 통신 제공 📧 ② Email Server (메일 서버) * 이메일 송·수신 및 저장 * SMTP, POP3, IMAP 프로토콜 지원 * 스팸 및 악성메일 차단 * 기업 메일 시스템 운영 🗄️ ③ Database Server (데이터베이스 서버) * 기업 데이터를 안전하게 저장·관리 * SQL 조회 및 트랜잭션 처리 * 데이터 무결성과 보안 보장 * ERP, CRM, 전자상거래 등 핵심 시스템 운영 🌍 ④ DNS Server (DNS 서버) * 도메인 이름을 IP 주소로 변환 * 인터넷 주소 검색 지원 * DNS 캐시를 통한 성능 향상 * 안정적인 네트워크 연결 제공 📁 ⑤ File Server (파일 서버) * 중앙 집중형 파일 저장 * 사용자 권한 기반 접근 제어 * 백업 및 버전 관리 지원 * 조직 내 협업 효율 향상 📤 ⑥ FTP Server (FTP 서버) * 서버와 클라이언트 간 파일 전송 * 대용량 파일 업로드·다운로드 * 소프트웨어 배포 및 백업 활용 * SFTP/FTPS를 활용하면 더욱 안전한 전송 가능 🛡️ ⑦ Web Proxy Server (웹 프록시 서버) * 사용자와 인터넷 사이의 중계 서버 * 웹 캐싱으로 속도 향상 * 웹 필터링 및 접근 제어 * 악성 사이트 차단 및 보안 강화 📡 ⑧ DHCP Server (DHCP 서버) * IP 주소 자동 할당 * 서브넷 마스크, 게이트웨이, DNS 정보 자동 배포 * IP 충돌 방지 * 네트워크 관리 자동화 ⸻ ⭐ 왜 서버가 중요한가? ✔ 안정적인 서비스 운영 ✔ 네트워크 성능 최적화 ✔ 데이터 보호 및 접근 제어 ✔ 중앙 집중형 자원 관리 ✔ 장애 대응 및 서비스 연속성 확보 ✔ 클라우드 및 AI 서비스의 기반 인프라 제공 오늘날 AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform(GCP) 역시 이러한 서버들을 가상화하여 제공하며, 현대적인 클라우드 환경에서는 웹 서버, 데이터베이스 서버, DNS 서버, 파일 서버 등이 유기적으로 연결되어 하나의 서비스 플랫폼을 구성합니다. 💡 네트워크를 배우는 것은 단순히 장비를 배우는 것이 아니라, 서버들이 어떻게 협력하여 하나의 서비스를 완성하는지를 이해하는 과정입니다. 서버의 역할을 이해하면 시스템 아키텍처 설계, 클라우드 구축, DevOps, 정보보안, AI 인프라까지 훨씬 쉽게 접근할 수 있습니다. 📌 저장해 두면 네트워크·클라우드·시스템 관리자·정보보안(ISO/IEC 27001, 27701, 42001)·AWS/Azure/GCP 자격증(AWS SAA, AZ-104, Google ACE) 학습 시 매우 유용한 핵심 정리 자료가 될 것입니다. Caption: 🚀 SQL Bootcamp 30 | Day 9 🎓 Learn SQL with 🧠 Indexes in SQL – Speed Up Your Queries As databases grow, query performance becomes critical. SQL Indexes help SQL Server find data quickly without scanning the entire table, making your queries faster and more efficient. 📚 What is an Index? An Index is a database object that improves the speed of data retrieval by creating a structured lookup on one or more columns. It mainly improves: SELECT WHERE JOIN ORDER BY GROUP BY ⚡ Types of Indexes 🔹 Clustered Index Stores table data in sorted order. Only one per table. Usually created on the PRIMARY KEY. Best for range queries. 🔹 Non-Clustered Index Stores index separately from table data. Contains pointers to actual rows. Multiple indexes allowed. Ideal for search operations. 🔹 Other SQL Indexes ✅ Unique Index ✅ Composite Index ✅ Filtered Index ✅ Full-Text Index ✅ XML Index ✅ Columnstore Index 💻 See It in Action CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_Employee_ID ON Employee(EmployeeID); CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Employee_Name ON Employee(EmployeeName); 🌍 Where Is It Used? 🏦 Banking & Financial Systems 🛒 E-Commerce Platforms 📊 Business Intelligence ☁️ Data Warehousing 🔄 ETL & Data Engineering 🏥 Healthcare Applications ⭐ Why Use Indexes? ✔ Faster query execution ✔ Improves JOIN performance ✔ Optimizes WHERE filtering ✔ Speeds up ORDER BY & GROUP BY ✔ Reduces table scans ✔ Improves reporting performance ✔ Better application response time 🚫 Common Mistakes ❌ Creating indexes on every column ❌ Too many indexes affecting INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ❌ Ignoring fragmented indexes ❌ Creating duplicate indexes ❌ Indexing rarely used columns 💎 Pro SQL Tip Create indexes only on columns frequently used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY clauses. Caption: Inside Kafka Architecture: Brokers, Topics, Partitions, and Replication Apache Kafka powers some of the world's largest real-time data platforms by combining scalability, reliability, and high-performance event streaming. Understanding its architecture is the first step toward building resilient distributed systems. Here's a quick breakdown: Brokers: Store data, manage client requests, and coordinate cluster operations. Topics: Organize events into logical streams for producers and consumers. Partitions: Split topics into smaller units, enabling parallel processing and horizontal scalability. Replication: Creates multiple copies of partition data across brokers, ensuring fault tolerance and high availability. Leader & Follower Model: Each partition has one leader handling reads/writes, while followers replicate data for automatic failover. Offsets: Every message receives a unique offset, allowing reliable message tracking and replay. Kafka's distributed design delivers high throughput, durability, low latency, and fault tolerance, making it the preferred platform for event-driven architectures, microservices, IoT, and real-time analytics. Caption: My agents now have a brain. Every decision, every problem, every reason we did it that way. Lose that and six months later you've got no idea why you built it like this. So I built The Brain, my own long-term memory system for coding agents. Here's how it actually works: It's just markdown files on disk. No database schema, no lock-in. Agents write straight into it themselves, using skills that know exactly where each thing belongs. Decisions get a card, not just an outcome. The brief, the options I was given, which one I picked and why. Shown right there in Mission Control, my own UI. Learnings get dropped in too. Post-mortems, techniques, problems solved. The moment we learn something, it goes straight in the folder. Everything's indexed on a vector database. A file watcher runs it through Google's newest embeddings model the second it lands. Multimodal, so video, audio and photos index too, not just text. Files link themselves, Obsidian-style. Drop a text file in and it searches the database for anything related, then adds those as links in the footer automatically. Media gets a sidecar file. Images, video, audio. We transcribe it and write the gist to a markdown sidecar, which gets indexed right alongside the file itself. The result: observational memory, forever. Borrowed the pattern from Mastra, built my own vector brain on top of it. It goes with me, computer to computer, wherever I build next. Full walkthrough on the channel. Building in public, as ever. Caption: What if every deployment could be traced back to a single source of truth? That's one of the things I've been learning about while exploring GitOps. Instead of relying on manual deployments or making changes directly in production, GitOps uses Git as the single source of truth for both infrastructure and application deployments. What I find particularly interesting about this approach is that every change is version-controlled, traceable, and easier to reproduce. A typical GitOps workflow might look like this: ❖ A developer opens a pull request. ❖ Changes are reviewed and merged into Git. ❖ GitHub Actions builds and validates the application. ❖ Argo CD synchronises the desired state to the Kubernetes cluster. ❖ Monitoring tools such as Prometheus help detect issues, while rollback strategies can help minimise the impact of failed deployments. As I continue building hands-on projects with GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Terraform, Docker, and Argo CD, I'm learning that DevOps isn't simply about deploying faster. It's about building systems that are: ❖ Reliable ❖ Repeatable ❖ Secure ❖ Easier to maintain Every new concept I learn reminds me that automation should not only improve speed but also improve confidence in the deployment process. ❖ I'd love to hear from the community: ❖ Have you adopted GitOps in your projects or workplace? ❖ What has been the biggest benefit or challenge you've experienced? ❖ If you haven't explored GitOps yet, what's stopping you from getting started?
